clinicalPearls: An enteric neuromuscular disorder in which the myenteric and submucosal plexuses are dysplastic rather than absent, mimicking Hirschsprung disease
Presents in infancy or childhood with chronic constipation, abdominal distension, and features of functional obstruction
The commoner form (type B) is characterised by hyperplasia of the submucosal plexus with giant ganglia and ectopic ganglion cells
It can occur in isolation or alongside true aganglionosis, sometimes proximal to a Hirschsprung segment
Diagnosis requires full-thickness or deep rectal biopsy with specialised histochemistry and immunohistochemistry, and is subject to interobserver variability
Management is largely conservative with bowel-management measures, reserving surgery for refractory or clearly localised disease
The diagnosis remains debated, with evolving histological criteria and uncertain reproducibility
reference.pathophysiology: Intestinal neuronal dysplasia is a form of enteric dysganglionosis in which ganglion cells are present but abnormally organised. In the classic type B pattern there is hyperplasia of the submucosal (and myenteric) plexus with giant ganglia, increased ganglion cell numbers, and ectopic neurons within the lamina propria and around submucosal vessels, together with abnormal acetylcholinesterase activity. This disordered innervation impairs coordinated peristalsis, producing a functional obstruction that clinically resembles Hirschsprung disease despite the presence of ganglion cells.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Full-thickness or deep suction rectal biopsy with acetylcholinesterase histochemistry and immunohistochemistry
Contrast enema to assess calibre change and transition zone
Anorectal manometry to assess the rectoanal inhibitory reflex
Abdominal radiography to evaluate distension and obstruction
Assessment for associated aganglionosis or systemic neuromuscular disease
redFlags: Features of complete or worsening intestinal obstruction
Enterocolitis with sepsis, particularly where Hirschsprung disease coexists
Failure to thrive or severe malnutrition
Bowel ischaemia or perforation from chronic distension
reference.prognosis: Many children improve over time with conservative bowel management, and outcome depends on the extent of disease and whether aganglionosis coexists; the uncertain diagnostic criteria complicate prognostication.
pitfalls: Confidently diagnosing or excluding the condition despite substantial interobserver variability in histology
Missing coexisting Hirschsprung aganglionosis in the distal segment
Proceeding to resection when conservative management would suffice
Interpreting inadequate or superficial biopsies as definitive
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Establish a conservative bowel-management programme with laxatives, enemas and dietary fibre as the mainstay
Use regular rectal washouts for refractory constipation and functional obstruction
Provide nutritional support and management of abdominal distension
Reserve surgery such as myectomy or resection for clearly localised or refractory disease
Exclude and manage coexisting Hirschsprung aganglionosis, which alters the surgical approach
Follow up through paediatric gastroenterology and surgery with periodic reassessment, as many children improve over time
